sq.q: Prove that the Z-transform of the sequence \(\frac{1}{n}\) (for \(n>0\) is \(Z [\frac{1}{n}]\) = \(\log\frac{z}{z-1}\) .
answer: Start with the unilateral Z-transform \(Z[\frac{1}{n}] = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} z^{-n} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n}(\frac{1}{z})^n\)
Use the power series expansion \(-\ln(1 - x) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{x^{n}}{n} \) with \(x=\frac{1}{z} \) . Thus \(Z[\frac{1}{n}]=-\ln(1-\frac{1}{z})= \ln(\frac{z}{z-1})\) .

lq.q: Derive the Z-transforms of the sequences \(1, a^n \) and \(n\) .State the region of convergence for each and briefly explain the principle used.
answer: Unilateral Z-transform: \(Z\{f(n)\} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} f(n) z^{-n} \) , convergence determined by values of zzz for which the series converges.

\(Z\{1\} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} z^{-n} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac{1}{z}\right)^n \) .This is a geometric series with ratio \(x=\frac{1}{x}\) . For \(|x|<1\) the sum is \((1-x)^{-1}\) .Hence \(Z\{1\} = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{1}{z}} = \frac{z}{z - 1} \) .Region of convergence \(|\frac{1}{z}|<1 \implies |z|>1\) .
Again a geometric series with ratio \(x = \frac{a}{z}\) .For \(|x|<1, Z\{a^n\} = \frac{1}{1 - \frac{a}{z}} = \frac{z}{z - a} \) .

Start from the known power-series identity (for \( |x| < 1\) ): \({Z}\{n\} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n z^{-n} = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} n \left(\frac{1}{z}\right)^n = \frac{\frac{1}{z}}{\left(1-\frac{1}{z}\right)^2}. \)
